method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar ended last week at its highest since April 2025 because Federal Reserve officials, from usually cautious San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly to Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, kept saying inflation is too high and rates must rise again; markets see a December rise as close to certain and Bank of America expects more in January and March. A Trump–Xi–Putin meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday is the week's wild card, though officials expect no deal.

EUR.text: The euro closed last week near $1.103, its lowest since April 2025, as talk of more US rate rises lifted the dollar. Germany's central bank chief Joachim Nagel says another European Central Bank rise is very likely, but markets expect December's to be the last while the Fed keeps going, which still favours the dollar.

JPY.text: The dollar sits just under 160 yen because US rates are far above Japan's, and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama has warned Tokyo will act against fast moves. Japan's economy shrank slightly in July to September, which gives the Bank of Japan a reason to wait beyond December, though the yen barely moved on the figures.

CHF.text: The Swiss franc slipped to a one-month low against a dollar lifted by bets on more Federal Reserve rate rises. Gulf attacks and an Israeli cabinet meeting on Iran keep some demand for the franc as a safe place, but a calm market open and a possible pause in US strikes point the other way.

CAD.text: Oil, Canada's main export, is near $96 and weekend attacks on Gulf shipping and Saudi Arabia add support, while the Bank of Canada says it is ready to raise rates again if energy costs spread. But Canada has lost jobs two months running and the strong US dollar holds the loonie down; October inflation on Monday morning is the next guide.

AUD.text: The Australian dollar has been the weakest major currency this past month, as Australia is the only big economy where markets expect rate cuts next year while US rate rises lift the US dollar. China's October factory, spending and investment figures all fell short of forecasts, a fresh sign of softer demand from Australia's biggest customer.

NZD.text: The New Zealand dollar gave back all of its rise after the November 7 election and sits near 55 US cents, held down by the strong US dollar. Weak Chinese shop sales in October add to the pressure, since China is a big buyer of New Zealand's food exports.

XAU.text: Gold is heading for a weekly loss of about 4.5%, near $3,880 an ounce and its lowest in over a year, because markets see a December Federal Reserve rate rise as close to certain and 10-year US bond yields sit above 5%. Demand from the Middle East war has not been enough to offset that.

OIL.text: Oil is drifting lower, near $95 for Brent, after two weekly falls, because the International Energy Agency now expects more supply than demand this quarter and emergency stocks are ready to be released. Iran's unconfirmed claims of tankers hit by mines near Hormuz, and an Israeli cabinet weighing new strikes, keep some war risk in the price, and weak Chinese data adds to the softer demand picture.

items.headline: China Industrial Output Slows to 4.8%, Retail Sales Growth Falls to 0.4%
items.story_title: The week's first numbers: Japan, China and Canada
items.summary: China's October figures for factory output, shop sales and investment all came in weaker than forecast, pointing to softer demand from the world's second-largest economy.

beats.was: China buys much of Australia's iron ore and much of New Zealand's farm exports, so its monthly spending and factory figures move both currencies. The economy grew 4.5% a year in July to September, better than expected.
beats.happened: Factory output grew 4.8% from a year earlier, down from 5.5% in September and below the 5.3% forecast. Retail sales rose just 0.4%, under the 0.8% expected, and investment in buildings and equipment fell 8.1% so far this year, a deeper drop than forecast, with property investment down more than a fifth. The statistics bureau said supply is still running well ahead of demand.
beats.means: Chinese households and businesses are holding back, and exports are doing most of the work. That raises the odds Beijing adds more support, but for now it means less demand for the raw materials Australia and New Zealand sell.
beats.fx: Negative for the Australian dollar, the currency most tied to Chinese demand, and mildly for the New Zealand dollar. A softer China also takes a little away from oil demand.

impact.why: All three main October measures missed, a clear sign of weaker demand from Australia's biggest customer.
Weak Chinese shop sales point to softer demand for New Zealand's food exports.
Slower factory and building activity in the biggest oil importer trims the demand outlook.

items.watch: Thursday's Trump–Xi–Putin meeting in Shenzhen; any sign of new Chinese spending support or trade relief would ease the hit to the Australian dollar.

items.headline: Oil prices fall on expectations of coming supply surplus
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Oil kept slipping early Monday in Asia as the market leaned on a forecast that supply will outrun demand this quarter, despite a new Iranian claim of a tanker hitting a mine.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since February and traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf's main oil route, is badly disrupted. Last week the International Energy Agency, which advises rich countries on energy, switched its view for October to December from a shortage to a surplus.
beats.happened: Brent, the world benchmark, fell about half a percent to near $95.40 a barrel and US crude eased to about $88.30. The agency expects supply to beat demand by 1.7 million barrels a day this quarter and says 71 million barrels of emergency stocks can be released by the end of February. Iran's navy said a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine east of Hormuz, which could not be confirmed, and the White House extended a shipping-rule waiver that eases US fuel deliveries.
beats.means: Traders are giving more weight to the expected surplus and emergency stocks than to new war claims. High shipping costs still keep a floor under prices, so oil is drifting rather than falling hard.
beats.fx: A slightly softer oil price takes a little support from the Canadian dollar and helps oil importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: An expected surplus and emergency stocks outweigh an unconfirmed tanker claim.
Softer prices for Canada's main export.

items.watch: Proof from ship trackers or insurers that the tanker was hit; confirmed damage would bring war risk back into oil.

items.headline: Iran says it will not wait for the US to attack first
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Iran will not wait to be attacked and suggested US diplomacy is cover to prepare new strikes. He also said UN nuclear inspectors stay locked out for now.

beats.was: Iran and the US have been at war since February, with Iran mining the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil. A June deal opened a 60-day window for talks that has now run out.
beats.happened: Gharibabadi said the Revolutionary Guards are building missiles with longer ranges and will not let the International Atomic Energy Agency, the UN nuclear watchdog, into nuclear sites until Iran's conditions are met. The same day Yemen's Houthis claimed drone hits on pumping stations of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which Saudi Arabia did not confirm.
beats.means: Tehran is talking tougher just as Trump weighs pausing strikes, so the risk of a fresh round of fighting has not gone away. The East-West pipeline matters because it lets Saudi oil skip Hormuz.
beats.fx: Keeps a war premium in oil, mildly helping the Canadian dollar and hurting oil importers like Japan; adds a little safe-place demand for the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Harder Iranian line and unconfirmed pipeline claims keep supply worries alive.
Threat of new fighting adds some safe-place demand.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so higher prices hurt.

items.watch: Whether Saudi Arabia confirms any damage to the East-West pipeline, and what comes out of Iran's foreign minister's Oman visit on Tuesday.

items.headline: Saudi Arabia intercepts Houthi missiles targeting Riyadh as Iran claims Bahrain drone attack
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Saudi air defences shot down two ballistic missiles that Yemen's Houthis fired at Riyadh on Sunday, plus drones over the oil-rich Eastern Province. Nothing was reported hit.

beats.was: Iran and the US have been at war since February, and Yemen's Houthis, who are backed by Iran, have been firing at Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil exporter. Last week Houthi strikes on Saudi energy sites added about $3 to the oil price in a day.
beats.happened: The spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said two Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at the Saudi capital were destroyed, along with drones over the Eastern Province, where most Saudi oil is pumped. It came the same morning Bahrain said it stopped Iranian drones aimed at a US radar site.
beats.means: No damage this time, but the Houthis are now aiming at the capital and the oil region on the same day, and the Group of Seven rich nations condemned the attacks. A hit on Saudi oil sites would matter far more than another failed attack.
beats.fx: Keeps a small war premium in oil, which supports the Canadian dollar and weighs on big oil importers like Japan and the euro area; the Swiss franc gets a little safe-place demand.

impact.why: Attacks on Saudi Arabia keep supply risk alive, though nothing was hit.
More Gulf attacks add some demand for a safe place to hold money.
Firmer oil helps Canada's main export.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so higher prices hurt.

items.watch: Whether any Houthi missile or drone gets through to a Saudi oil site, and whether the Gulf calms around Iran's foreign minister's trip to Oman on Tuesday.

items.headline: Yemen government forces withdraw from area near Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Houthis in control
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces pulled back on Sunday from the area overlooking Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow southern entrance to the Red Sea, leaving Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in control of its shore.

beats.was: Bab el-Mandeb links the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean and carries Gulf oil shipped from Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port of Yanbu, the main way around a mostly shut Hormuz. The Houthis, allied with Iran, have already struck Yanbu and other Saudi oil sites, and the government began an offensive in October to retake the coast.
beats.happened: Southern forces fighting for Yemen's recognised government said they were leaving the Dhubab airport and Bab el-Mandeb area west of Taiz to move toward Aden and defend it, as the Houthis press into the south. Reuters calls it a major setback for the government side.
beats.means: The Houthis now overlook both sides of the Gulf's escape routes problem: with Hormuz mostly shut, the Red Sea is the main bypass, and the group gains more power to threaten it. They have not announced new attacks on ships, so this raises risk rather than cutting supply today.
beats.fx: Adds to oil's war premium and to demand for safe places to hold money such as the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Iran-aligned rebels gain control over the Red Sea route that carries oil around a mostly shut Hormuz.
A wider Gulf war adds demand for a safe place to hold money.
Higher oil prices help Canada's main export.

items.watch: Whether the Houthis warn or attack ships in the Red Sea, and whether shipping firms reroute away from it.

items.headline: Japan Q3 GDP shrinks 0.1% annualised vs +0.3% expected as exports and consumers weigh
items.story_title: Will the Bank of Japan raise rates in December?
items.summary: Japan's economy shrank slightly in July to September, the first fall in a year, as households spent less and exports slipped.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan holds its key rate at 1.25% and markets expect a rise to 1.5% at its December meeting. The dollar has been trading just under 160 yen, a level where Tokyo has stepped in before.
beats.happened: The government's first estimate shows the economy shrank at a 0.1% yearly pace in the third quarter, against forecasts of a small rise. Household spending fell for the quarter and trade subtracted from growth, while business investment rose more than expected. A broad measure of price pressure also came in softer than forecast.
beats.means: A shrinking economy and softer prices give the more cautious Bank of Japan members a reason to wait. Strong business investment keeps the case for a December rise alive, so the figures blur the picture rather than settle it.
beats.fx: Mildly negative for the yen, since anything that delays a Japanese rate rise keeps the gap with US rates wide. The yen barely moved at first.

impact.why: A weak quarter gives the Bank of Japan a reason to delay its December rise.
Keeps the wide gap between US and Japanese rates in place against the yen.

items.watch: Bank of Japan board member Hajime Takata speaks Monday; if he still backs a December rise, the weak quarter matters less.

items.headline: US futures open firmer as Nasdaq leads, oil slips despite Iran tanker claims: 5 things
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Oil opened the week slightly lower and US stock futures rose, even after Iran said a supertanker sank near the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since February, and Iran has claimed several tankers hit mines near Hormuz, the narrow route for much of the Gulf's oil. Brent crude, the world benchmark, ended last week near $96 after two weekly falls.
beats.happened: When trading reopened Sunday evening US time, Brent slipped below $96 and US crude was flat near $87. Iran's claim that a supertanker sank has not been confirmed, and a third US aircraft carrier group is reported to have joined the two already in the region. Gold was steady near $3,890.
beats.means: Traders are not adding much to oil on Iran's claims alone; they want proof of lost supply. A calm open suggests the weekend's attacks did not change the view that supply is running ahead of demand.
beats.fx: A soft oil price takes a little support from the Canadian dollar and eases pressure on oil importers like Japan. Firmer stocks point to a steady mood, which does little for safe places like the franc.

impact.why: Unconfirmed tanker claims did not lift prices at the open.
Slightly softer oil, Canada's main export.
Rising stock futures point to less demand for safe places.

items.watch: Confirmation, from ship trackers or insurers, that a tanker actually sank would bring war risk back into oil.

items.headline: Iran targets Bahrain again as Trump weighs a pause in strikes
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: President Trump has signalled he may hold off on new US strikes on Iran if Tehran and Yemen's Houthis stop provoking, though the US naval blockade of Iran stays in place.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since February, and the US Navy blocks Iran's oil exports. On Thursday Trump said the US no longer needs a deal with Iran and took Vice President JD Vance off the talks.
beats.happened: Reuters reports Trump may pause strikes as long as Iran and the Houthis hold back, while Israeli officials keep pressing Washington to hit Iran again. Over the weekend Iran still claimed drone attacks on a US radar in Bahrain and said more tankers hit mines near Hormuz.
beats.means: It is a conditional pause, not a ceasefire, and the weekend attacks already test the condition. The blockade staying means Iranian oil stays off the market either way.
beats.fx: A pause would take a little war risk out of oil, which mildly weighs on the Canadian dollar and helps oil importers like Japan; a breakdown would do the opposite.

impact.why: Fewer US strikes would ease supply fears, but the blockade and Gulf attacks continue.
Safe-place demand eases only if both sides actually hold back.

items.watch: Whether Iran or the Houthis launch new attacks before Iran's foreign minister visits Oman on Tuesday, which would likely end the pause.

items.headline: Mossad chief returns from US Iran talks as Israeli security cabinet convenes
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Israel's top security ministers met Sunday evening for the first time since the election, after the head of its spy agency briefed Washington on Iran.

beats.was: Israel's caretaker government under Benjamin Netanyahu wants the US to resume strikes on Iran, while President Trump has signalled he may hold off. Gadi Eisenkot, who is forming Israel's next government, has urged restraint.
beats.happened: Mossad head Roman Gofman returned from Washington after briefing senior US officials, including CIA Director John Ratcliffe, on Israel's latest intelligence about Iran. The security cabinet, the group of ministers that can approve military action, then met for the first time since early October. No decision to attack has been announced.
beats.means: Israel is pushing for more military action at the same time Washington talks of a pause, so the two allies are not fully in step. A meeting that could approve strikes keeps the risk of a wider war on the table.
beats.fx: Any sign of new Israeli strikes would lift oil and safe places like the Swiss franc and gold. Silence from the meeting would let that risk fade.

impact.why: A possible new strike on Iran keeps supply risk alive.
War risk adds a little demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Any statement after the meeting approving action, or US pushback; Iran's foreign minister visits Oman on Tuesday.

items.headline: Iran says supertanker carrying oil sinks in Hormuz Strait
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude sank on Sunday after hitting a mine near the Strait of Hormuz, one of two tankers they say were hit. No one outside Iran has confirmed the sinking.

beats.was: Since the war with the US began in February, Iran has let ships through Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, only with its permission, while the US blockades Iran's ports and escorts tankers. Iran said three tankers hit mines on Saturday.
beats.happened: In a statement on state TV, the Guards said two tankers on an unapproved route hit mines in the south of the strait and one, a supertanker, went down; they gave no names. Separately, the UK Navy's shipping-warning office, relaying Indian authorities, reported a tanker attacked in the Gulf just before the strait, with the crew safe and damage unknown.
beats.means: A sunk supertanker would be the worst ship loss of the recent attacks and a sign that US mine clearing has not made the route safe. Because the claim is unconfirmed and Iran has made similar claims before, markets may wait for ship owners or trackers before reacting fully.
beats.fx: Adds to the war premium in oil when trading resumes Sunday evening US time, which helps the Canadian dollar and costs big energy importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: A claimed sinking and a confirmed tanker attack show the main Gulf oil route is still unsafe.
Dearer oil helps Canada's main export.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a higher bill hurts.
Gulf escalation adds demand for a safe place to hold money.

items.watch: Whether ship owners or tracking firms name the ship and confirm it sank, and how Brent opens Sunday evening US time.

items.headline: Iranian foreign minister to visit Oman on Tuesday for talks with counterpart
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi will fly to Oman on Tuesday for talks with Oman's foreign minister. It is the first planned diplomatic step after a weekend of mine and drone attacks around the Gulf.

beats.was: Iran and the US have been at war since February. Oman, which sits on the south side of the Strait of Hormuz, has long carried messages between Tehran and Washington, but President Trump said last week the US does not need a deal with Iran.
beats.happened: Iran's state news agency, quoting Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, said Araghchi will hold talks in Muscat on Tuesday. No agenda was given; US coverage links the trip to Oman's role in talks on who oversees Hormuz shipping.
beats.means: A visit is not a negotiation, but it shows a channel for talks is still open even as Iran claims new tanker hits and strikes on Bahrain. Any sign of US involvement would be the first easing since the talks stalled.
beats.fx: A small offset to the weekend's war premium: if the trip produces talk of safer shipping, oil could ease, which would help Japan and the euro area and take a little support from the Canadian dollar.

impact.why: An open diplomatic channel slightly lowers the odds of a long shipping shutdown.
Japan gains if oil import costs ease.
Less war premium in oil means less help for Canada's main export.

items.watch: Whether Oman or Iran says US officials are part of Tuesday's talks, and whether attacks on shipping pause around the visit.

items.headline: Bahrain warns Iran against turning kingdom into 'arena for scores'
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Bahrain blamed Iran for Sunday's drone attacks and said it keeps the right to respond, while Saudi Arabia and the head of the Gulf Cooperation Council, the six-nation Gulf alliance, said an attack on one member is an attack on all.

beats.was: Bahrain, a small Gulf kingdom that hosts the US Navy's regional headquarters, has stayed mostly out of the fighting since the US–Iran war began in February. Late Saturday Iran's Revolutionary Guards said their drones hit a US radar at a Bahraini base.
beats.happened: On Sunday Bahrain's Foreign Ministry rejected Iran's reasons for the attack, said the country will not become a battleground for other people's quarrels, held Tehran responsible and said it would coordinate its defence with fellow Gulf states under their joint defence pact. Saudi Arabia backed Bahrain, and Gulf Cooperation Council chief Jasem Albudaiwi called the drones a direct threat to the whole region. Neither the US nor Bahrain has confirmed that the radar was hit.
beats.means: Words of solidarity are expected, but the talk of joint defence raises the chance that more Gulf states are drawn in if Iran keeps striking. That widens the risk to the region's oil output, not just to ships in Hormuz.
beats.fx: A small extra push for oil and for safe places to hold money such as the Swiss franc; on its own it changes little, since markets already know of the attacks.

impact.why: A wider Gulf front puts more oil output at risk.
Rising regional tension adds some demand for a safe currency.
Any oil premium helps Canada's main export.

items.watch: Whether Gulf states act together against Iran beyond statements, or Iran stops its strikes on Bahrain.

items.headline: Bahrain issues first nationwide alert in months as Iran claims attack on base hosting US helicopters
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Bahrain told everyone in the country to take shelter on Sunday after Iran's Revolutionary Guards said their drones hit a US radar at a Bahraini base; Bahrain's military says its air defences stopped the attacks. Saudi Arabia also shot down missiles fired at Riyadh by Yemen's Houthi rebels.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since February, with the US blockading Iranian ports and Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, mostly shut. Bahrain hosts the US Navy's main Gulf base, and Iran claimed a strike on a US radar there on Friday.
beats.happened: Late Saturday the Guards said six drones hit a US air-defence radar at the Riffa helicopter base. Early Sunday Bahrain's Interior Ministry issued its first country-wide alerts in months and explosions were heard, and Bahrain's Defence Force later said it had shot down several Iranian attacks before they reached their targets, its first such interceptions since September. Washington has not commented on Sunday's claim. Saudi Arabia said it destroyed two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh and drones over its oil-rich Eastern Region.
beats.means: Attacks on a US base and on Saudi Arabia over two days point to the war widening beyond shipping, which makes an early reopening of Hormuz less likely. Bahrain's account suggests little damage, and oil fell last week despite similar news.
beats.fx: Adds to the war premium in oil when markets reopen Sunday evening US time, and to demand for safe places to hold money such as the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Strikes reaching a US base and Saudi Arabia over a weekend raise the risk to Gulf supply.
War news adds to demand for the franc as a safe place to hold money.
Higher oil helps Canada, a big oil exporter.

items.watch: Whether the US confirms damage or answers, and how oil opens on Sunday evening US time.

items.headline: Iran: 3 oil tankers hit naval mines in Strait of Hormuz
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's navy and Revolutionary Guards say three oil tankers, one of them a supertanker, caught fire on Saturday after hitting mines in and near the Strait of Hormuz. No ship names were given and the claims are unconfirmed.

beats.was: Since the war with the US began in February, Iran has required ships to get its permission to pass through Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. The US says it has cleared the main routes of mines, and Iran said an LNG tanker hit a mine on Friday.
beats.happened: The Guards said two tankers that had switched off their tracking to take an unapproved route exploded and caught fire in the south of the strait, and two others turned back after warnings. Iran's regular navy said a third tanker east of the strait hit a mine and stopped, and warned that any ship breaking its rules will be set on fire.
beats.means: If true, it is the third weekly round of ship attacks and a sign that Iran can still stop traffic despite US mine clearing, which keeps the strait mostly shut. Without names or outside confirmation, it is weaker evidence than last week's hits.
beats.fx: Supports oil when trading resumes, a help for the Canadian dollar and a cost for big energy importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: More tankers hit in the main Gulf oil route keep supply at risk.
Dearer oil helps Canada's main export.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a higher bill hurts.

items.watch: Whether shipping trackers or ship owners confirm the hits, and whether insurers raise rates for Gulf voyages.

items.headline: 'New Yalta'? Trump and Putin push meeting that Xi is wary of hosting
items.story_title: Trump, Xi and Putin meet in Shenzhen on November 19
items.summary: US President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin are set to meet in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, November 19, but there is still no agenda, and Beijing is said to be uneasy about hosting.

beats.was: The three leaders have never met together. The talks are planned around the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which China hosts in Shenzhen this month, while the US and Israel are at war with Iran.
beats.happened: The White House said on Friday that nuclear arms cuts and the Iran war would be discussed, and the Kremlin confirmed the date. By Saturday no format had been set: Xi is reported to be wary of hosting, a US official said Trump is unlikely to raise the war in Ukraine, and Beijing has little interest in nuclear arms talks. A US official said no agreement is expected.
beats.means: A first meeting of the three most powerful leaders could calm or unsettle markets depending on what comes out of it, but with low expectations set in advance, the bar for a surprise is high. Any sign of a path to ending the Iran war would matter most, for oil.
beats.fx: Little effect until Thursday. A hint of progress on Iran would weigh on oil and help the Australian dollar through China; a public falling-out would do the reverse.

impact.why: Iran is on the list, but officials expect no deal, so oil waits for what is said.
Australia sells heavily to China, so the tone of US–China ties feeds through to the Australian dollar.

items.watch: Whether an agenda is published before Thursday, and anything said about the Iran war or trade during or after the meeting.

items.headline: Daily roundup: NZD gives back its post-election rise
items.story_title: New Zealand's election and the kiwi
items.summary: The New Zealand dollar ended the week near 55.2 US cents, having given back all of Monday's rise after the November 7 election.

beats.was: New Zealand voted on Saturday, November 7. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's National Party won 42 seats on the early count, and his three-party bloc looks set for 67 of 131 seats, just enough to govern. The final result is due November 27.
beats.happened: The kiwi jumped about 1.5% on Monday on relief at the result, then slid back through the week as the US dollar strengthened, ending Friday down 0.4% on the day at about $0.552.
beats.means: The election lift did not last: the strong dollar and US rate talk mattered more than the result at home. New Zealand's high jobless rate also gives the currency little support of its own.
beats.fx: Leaves the kiwi back where it started the week, at the mercy of the US dollar.

impact.why: Its post-election rise fully reversed as the US dollar firmed.

items.watch: The official vote count on November 27, and China's activity data, a big buyer of New Zealand goods.

items.headline: Week ahead: Japan GDP and China activity data open the week
items.story_title: The week's first numbers: Japan, China and Canada
items.summary: The week starts Sunday evening US time with Japan's first estimate of third-quarter growth and China's October spending and factory figures, then Canada's inflation on Monday morning.

beats.was: The yen is near 160 per dollar and the Bank of Japan is weighing a December rate rise; China's economy drives demand for Australian and New Zealand exports.
beats.happened: Japan's GDP is due at 6:50 PM US Central time on Sunday, forecast to show growth of just 0.1% over the quarter. China's October retail sales (forecast up 0.8% on a year earlier) and factory output (up 5.3%) follow at 8:00 PM. Canada's October consumer prices come at 7:30 AM on Monday.
beats.means: Weak Japanese growth would make a December Bank of Japan rise harder to justify, and soft Chinese shop spending would add to worries about demand there.
beats.fx: A weak Japanese number weighs on the yen; Chinese spending figures matter most for the Australian and New Zealand dollars; Canada's inflation sets the tone for the loonie.

impact.why: Growth near zero would make a December Bank of Japan rise harder to justify.
China's spending and factory figures feed directly into demand for Australian exports.
Monday's inflation figures shape talk of another Bank of Canada rise.

items.watch: Whether Japan's growth misses the 0.1% forecast, and how far Chinese retail sales stay near flat.

items.headline: Security Cabinet to Meet on Iran Amid Caretaker Debate
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Israel's security cabinet meets on Sunday for the first time since early October, after reports it told the army to be ready for a possible new strike on Iran.

beats.was: Israel and the US are at war with Iran, and attacks on Gulf oil sites and ships near the Strait of Hormuz have kept oil near $96 a barrel. Israel held an election this month, so Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu leads a caretaker government until a new one forms.
beats.happened: The cabinet, which handles war decisions, meets Sunday, November 15. The open question is whether a caretaker government can order a fresh strike on Iran. Gadi Eisenkot, who has been asked to form the next government, warned Netanyahu against major security moves during the handover.
beats.means: A meeting is not a decision, but it raises the chance of a new round of fighting at a time when oil had been drifting lower on hopes of calm. Eisenkot's pushback is a brake on that.
beats.fx: A small lift for oil and safe places to hold money, like the Swiss franc and gold, until it is clear what, if anything, was decided.

impact.why: Talk of a new Israeli strike on Iran raises the risk to Gulf supply.
Fresh war risk tends to draw money into the franc.

items.watch: Any report of what the cabinet decided, and whether oil opens higher when trading resumes Sunday evening US time.

items.headline: Fed's Jefferson says he is taking his policy cues from inflation
items.story_title: Fed: a December rate rise and what US inflation says
items.summary: Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said the path of inflation matters more to him than other signals, which suggests he could back more rate rises, though he gave no sense of pace.

beats.was: The Fed raised rates in September and held in October, when Jefferson voted with the majority. Markets expect a quarter-point rise at the December 8–9 meeting because inflation has stayed too high.
beats.happened: On Friday Jefferson said he sees inflation as the more important guide for policy right now. He did not say how fast or how far rates should rise.
beats.means: The Fed's number two adds his voice to a week in which almost every official who spoke leaned toward raising rates again. It backs a December rise without pointing to a bigger one.
beats.fx: Mild support for the dollar, already priced; a small weight on gold.

impact.why: A senior Fed leader puts inflation first, matching what markets expect.
Higher expected US rates make holding gold costlier.

items.watch: Fed officials' comments this week and US retail sales, for any push toward a half-point rise.

items.headline: Friday close: dollar ends the week at a 19-month high
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The dollar ended Friday at its highest since April 2025, with the euro near $1.103 and the yen just under 160 per dollar, as US 10-year bond yields had their biggest weekly rise in 19 months.

beats.was: All week, Federal Reserve officials said inflation is too high and rates must rise again, and markets added bets on rises in December and January.
beats.happened: The dollar index, which tracks it against six major currencies, closed at about 103.4, up a quarter of a percent on the day. The euro fell to about $1.103, its lowest since April 2025, the pound closed near $1.32, and the dollar briefly passed 160 yen in Tokyo before ending at 159.8. US 10-year yields ended at 5.15%.
beats.means: The week ended with the dollar's strength intact going into the weekend, rather than fading on Friday as it sometimes does. Higher US yields are doing the work.
beats.fx: Dollar firm into the new week; the euro and yen are under the most pressure, with the yen close to the level where Japan has warned it could step in.

impact.why: It closed the week at a 19-month high on higher US yields.
It ended at its lowest since April 2025.
It ended just short of 160 per dollar, the level Japan has warned about.

items.watch: Whether US yields keep rising this week, and any Japanese action if the dollar holds above 160 yen.

items.headline: US producer prices rise further in October
items.story_title: Fed: a December rate rise and what US inflation says
items.summary: Prices that US businesses charge rose 0.3% in October, a touch below the 0.4% forecast, but were 6.5% higher than a year ago, the fastest yearly rise since late 2022. The usual core measure, without food and energy, rose 0.3% as expected.

beats.was: The producer price index, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, tracks what businesses get for their goods and services and often feeds into shop prices later. October's consumer inflation report, out earlier this week, came in hotter than expected, and the Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise rates again at its December 8–9 meeting.
beats.happened: The headline index rose 0.3% on the month after a 1.4% jump in September, which was revised higher. Goods rose 0.5%, led by food, while transport and warehousing costs rose 2%, with truck freight up almost 4%. The usual core measure, which leaves out food and energy, rose 0.3%, in line with forecasts, and is 5.0% higher than a year ago. A narrower measure that also leaves out shops' and wholesalers' margins rose a firmer 0.5%.
beats.means: Nothing here was a surprise in either direction: the main core reading matched forecasts, though the narrower measure shows business costs still climbing outside energy. That keeps a December rate rise on track without adding to the case for a bigger half-point move.
beats.fx: Supports the dollar by backing more Fed rate rises, and adds to pressure on gold, which earns no interest.

impact.why: Core business prices rose as expected, keeping a December rate rise on track; the softer headline limits the lift.
More expected Fed rises raise the cost of holding gold.

items.watch: Comments from Fed officials later Friday, including Boston's Susan Collins, Dallas's Lorie Logan and Governor Michelle Bowman, on whether December should be a quarter or a half point.

items.headline: CENTCOM denies Iran's claim of destroying US radar in Bahrain
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: US Central Command, which runs American forces in the Middle East, says Iran's two attack drones aimed at Bahrain were shot down, with no damage or injuries, rejecting Iran's claim that it destroyed a US radar there.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since earlier this year, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, is still badly disrupted. Early Friday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain, home of the US Navy's Fifth Fleet.
beats.happened: Central Command said on X that the Guards launched two one-way attack drones toward Bahrain and US forces downed both. The Guards had called their attack a reply to a strike on a telecom tower in Sirik, on Iran's Hormuz coast.
beats.means: Iran did try to hit a US target in a Gulf country, so the risk of a direct clash is real, but the attack failed, which makes an immediate US counter-strike less pressing. It takes some of the edge off Friday morning's worry.
beats.fx: Eases some of the extra war premium in oil and in safe places to park money such as the Swiss franc, though an attempted strike on a US base keeps that premium from fading fully.

impact.why: A failed attack lowers the damage, but Iran still tried to hit a US base.
Less damage than claimed trims demand for the franc as a safe place to hold money.

items.watch: Whether the US answers the attempted drone attack, and whether Israel acts on its order to prepare a possible strike on Iran.

items.headline: Oil prices set for second weekly decline as Trump sticks with Iran blockade
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Oil is heading for a second weekly fall of around 2%, even after this week's attacks near Hormuz, as the US keeps its pressure on Iran through a blockade rather than wider fighting.

beats.was: Oil soared earlier this year when the US-Iran war shut most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Prices then fell hard last week, Brent by about 16%, as Gulf exports recovered.
beats.happened: Brent and US crude were mixed on Friday and on track to lose about 2% on the week. Reports say President Donald Trump is sticking with the US blockade of Iranian ports, which traders read as steady pressure rather than a new escalation.
beats.means: Ship attacks and Iran's claimed strike on a US base in Bahrain keep a risk premium in prices, but more Gulf supply and a coming surplus, which the International Energy Agency flagged this week, are pulling the other way.
beats.fx: A softer oil week takes some support away from oil exporters like Canada and eases inflation worries a little for big importers like Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Prices are on course for a second weekly drop as supply recovers.
Weaker oil trims support for Canada's main export.

items.watch: Whether the US confirms or answers Iran's claimed strike in Bahrain; a direct clash would quickly reverse the decline.

items.headline: Iran says it targeted US radar site in Bahrain
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they hit a US early-warning radar in Bahrain, home of the US Navy's Fifth Fleet. Neither Washington nor Bahrain has confirmed it.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since earlier this year, with the US blockading Iranian ports and Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, mostly shut. Ship attacks in the strait have picked up again this month.
beats.happened: The Guards said the strike answered an air attack on a telecom tower in Sirik, on Iran's Hormuz coast, and called it a warning over flights and oil smuggling in the strait. Reuters says it is the first claimed Iranian attack on US forces in a Gulf country since early September. Israel's security cabinet has also told its military to prepare for a possible strike on Iran.
beats.means: If confirmed, the war is spreading back from shipping to direct hits on US bases, which makes a deal to reopen Hormuz harder. For now it is a claim, and oil had already priced in a lot of risk on Thursday.
beats.fx: Adds to the risk premium in oil and to demand for safe places to park money, such as the Swiss franc and gold, though a strong dollar is limiting gold for now.

impact.why: A claimed strike on a US base makes a quick reopening of Hormuz less likely.
War news adds to demand for the franc as a safe place to hold money.
Higher oil helps Canada, a big oil exporter.

items.watch: Whether the US confirms damage or strikes back, and whether Israel acts on its preparations.

items.headline: Gold faces weekly rout as high US yields fuel Fed rate hike bets
items.story_title: Gold: rising US rates vs war risk
items.summary: Gold is on course to lose about 4.5% this week, trading near $3,880 an ounce, close to its lowest in 13 months, as markets bet heavily on a US rate rise in December.

beats.was: Gold fell below $3,900 on Thursday after October's US consumer prices came in hotter than expected and Federal Reserve officials said rates need to rise further.
beats.happened: Gold edged up slightly on Friday but stayed near its low for the year of about $3,852. The 10-year US Treasury yield held near 5.15%, and futures put the chance of a December Fed rise at about 90%, with a small chance of a bigger half-point move.
beats.means: Gold pays no interest, so with safe US bonds paying over 5% and more rises expected, holders have less reason to keep it. The Middle East war has not been enough to offset that this week.
beats.fx: The same rate bets keep the dollar near its highest since April 2025; cheaper gold is a mild drag on Australia's export income.

impact.why: High US yields and Fed rise bets keep weighing on gold; this repeats the week's move.
A near-certain December Fed rise supports the dollar.

items.watch: Minutes of the Fed's October meeting on Wednesday, US retail sales, and whether Fed officials push for a half-point rise.

items.headline: Japan's finance minister vows action as yen breaches 160 threshold
items.story_title: Japan's fight to prop up the yen
items.summary: The dollar crossed 160 yen for the first time since early September, and Japan's Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama warned again that Tokyo will act against fast, one-sided moves, working with the US Treasury.

beats.was: When the yen weakened to about 164 per dollar this summer, Japan spent a record 15.4 trillion yen buying it back between July 30 and August 3, and the US joined in on July 31, its first yen purchase since 1998.
beats.happened: After US inflation data raised bets on more Federal Reserve rate rises, the dollar reached about 160.03 yen. Katayama said on Friday that recent moves have been one-sided and rapid and Japan will respond appropriately. Her top currency official, Atsushi Mimura, gave a similar warning on Thursday.
beats.means: Tokyo is signalling it could buy yen again, and mentioning the US Treasury hints a joint move is possible. But talk alone has not reversed the slide, because US interest rates are still far above Japan's.
beats.fx: The warnings put a soft ceiling near 160 yen per dollar and raise the chance of a sudden sharp drop in the dollar against the yen, while the rate gap keeps pushing the other way.

impact.why: The yen is at a level where Japan stepped in before, but the rate gap with the US still drags it lower.
Higher US rates lift the dollar, but a Japanese or joint purchase of yen would hit it.

items.watch: Whether Japan actually buys yen, US producer prices on Friday, and Bank of Japan signals ahead of its December meeting.

items.headline: BofA adds January Fed hike to forecast, says quarterly pace no longer enough
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: Bank of America's economists now expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates in December, January and March, three rises in a row, after October's hot consumer price report.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve's main rate is 3.75%–4.00% after a rise in September and a hold in October. Most banks expected rises spaced out every other meeting, starting at the December 8–9 meeting.
beats.happened: Bank of America's research team added a quarter-point rise at the late-January 2027 meeting to its forecast, on top of December and March, saying a slower pace is no longer enough to cool prices. It warned the rate could pass 5% if wages jump or companies push through big price increases. Goldman Sachs expects rises in December and March, and Deutsche Bank sees one at each of the next three meetings. Futures show about a 90% chance of a quarter-point rise in December.
beats.means: Big banks are moving their forecasts toward faster and longer Fed tightening, which puts a higher floor under US rates into early next year.
beats.fx: Supports the dollar, especially against currencies whose central banks are near the end of their rises or expected to cut, and weighs on gold.

impact.why: A major bank now expects back-to-back Fed rises, though markets were already leaning that way.
Higher expected US rates raise the cost of holding gold, which pays no interest.

items.watch: Whether other banks follow, and US retail sales and the Fed's preferred inflation gauge before the December 8–9 meeting.

items.headline: Fed likely to need to raise rates amid worsening inflation: Daly
items.story_title: Fed: a December rate rise and what US inflation says
items.summary: San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said on Friday that she leans toward the Fed raising rates again, because prices of services are rising too fast and tend to stay high.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve raised rates in September, held in October, and markets now expect quarter-point rises at its December 8–9 and January 26–27 meetings. Core consumer prices have risen about 0.3% a month for three months, faster than the 0.2% that fits the Fed's 2% goal.
beats.happened: Speaking at a forecasting event at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, Daly said her leaning is that a rate rise will likely be needed and she will weigh it with colleagues in December. Her worry is service prices outside housing, which are moving the wrong way. She called US shoppers surprisingly strong but said she is watching the holiday season for signs they are running out of money.
beats.means: One of the Fed's more cautious voices now also leans toward a December rise, so the week ends with almost every official who spoke pointing the same way. She gave no backing to a bigger half-point move.
beats.fx: Keeps support under the dollar into the weekend and adds a little more weight on gold.

impact.why: A usually cautious Fed official leans toward a December rise, matching what markets already expect.
Higher expected US rates make holding gold costlier.

items.watch: US retail sales and the Fed's preferred inflation gauge in the coming weeks, and whether consumer spending slows over the holidays as Daly warned.

items.headline: Bundesbank's Nagel says it is "highly probable" the ECB must hike again as December move is priced at 72%
items.story_title: European Central Bank: one more rate rise, then a pause?
items.summary: Joachim Nagel, head of Germany's central bank and a European Central Bank rate-setter, said another rate rise is very likely if things stay as they are. Markets already put the odds of a December rise at about 72%.

beats.was: Euro-area inflation jumped to about 4% in October, the highest in three years, mostly because the Gulf war pushed up energy prices. The European Central Bank raised rates in September and has been weighing one more.
beats.happened: Speaking at a bankers' conference in Frankfurt on Friday, Bundesbank President Nagel said a further rise is highly probable, pointing to stubborn underlying inflation and rising short-term inflation expectations.
beats.means: Germany's voice carries weight on the ECB's council, so this firms up a December rise. It does not change the bigger picture: markets expect the ECB to stop after December while the Fed keeps going.
beats.fx: Gives the euro a little support, but the gap with the US, where more rate rises are expected into next year, still favours the dollar.

impact.why: Firms up a December ECB rise, though markets had mostly priced it.
Narrows the rate gap slightly, but the Fed is still expected to go further.

items.watch: Euro-area final October inflation and any comment from ECB President Christine Lagarde on whether December is the last rise.

items.headline: Boston Fed's Collins Says Higher Rates May Raise Home Purchase and Building Costs
items.story_title: Fed: a December rate rise and what US inflation says
items.summary: Boston Fed President Susan Collins said beating inflation comes first, even if higher interest rates make homes dearer to buy and build for a while.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve is raising rates to fight inflation that has spread from energy into wider prices, and markets expect another rise at its December 8–9 meeting. US home sales fell in October to their lowest since 2010, with 30-year mortgage rates above 7%.
beats.happened: Opening the Boston Fed's yearly economics conference, this year on housing, Collins said tighter policy is sometimes needed to keep prices stable, even though it raises the cost of buying or building a home in the short run. She said stable prices help the housing market over time, and noted New England workers turning down jobs over housing costs.
beats.means: A voter on rates is saying the housing slump will not stop the Fed from raising rates further. That adds to the run of officials this week who want rates higher, and gives no sign the Fed is ready to pause.
beats.fx: Mildly supports the dollar by keeping a December rise and more after it on the table; it adds a little more pressure on gold.

impact.why: Another Fed official puts inflation ahead of the housing slump, backing more rate rises.
Higher expected US rates raise the cost of holding gold.

items.watch: Whether Fed Governor Michelle Bowman and San Francisco's Mary Daly, speaking later Friday, back a half-point December move or stick to a quarter point.

items.headline: Iran says tanker carrying LNG hit mine, suffered explosion in Hormuz
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say a ship carrying liquefied natural gas hit a sea mine and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday. No details on the ship have come out yet.

beats.was: The US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February, and Iran has since restricted the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil and much of its liquefied gas. Iran said four oil tankers were hit by explosions there on Wednesday and Thursday.
beats.happened: The Guards' navy said the gas carrier struck a mine after taking a route Iran calls unauthorized and dangerous; the claim came through Iranian state media and has not been checked. At least 10 ships were hit in the first 10 days of November, after 37 attacks in October, the most in any month since the war began.
beats.means: Iran keeps hitting ships that ignore its rules, even as overall traffic recovers. So far markets are looking past it: oil is still headed for a second weekly fall on more supply and hopes the war winds down.
beats.fx: Adds a little war risk to oil and gas prices, which helps the Canadian dollar and weighs on big energy importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Another ship hit in the main Gulf route, though prices barely reacted.
Europe relies on imported liquefied gas, so attacks on gas carriers raise its energy risk.
Japan imports nearly all its energy, including gas from the Gulf.

items.watch: Whether the ship's owner or another source confirms the hit, and whether shipping firms slow Hormuz trips again.

items.headline: Global oil market to return to surplus in Q4 2026, larger supply build expected in 2027: IEA
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: The International Energy Agency expects the world to produce more oil than it uses again in the last three months of this year, with a bigger surplus in 2027.

beats.was: The war around Hormuz cut Gulf exports sharply and pushed North Sea crude to about $136 a barrel in early October. Prices have since fallen by about a third as other producers pumped more.
beats.happened: In its monthly report, the IEA said world supply rose by 2.3 million barrels a day in October to 105.4 million, while demand this year is set to fall by 2.7 million barrels a day after the price spike. Gulf exports are still about a quarter below pre-war levels, and stocks held on land are the lowest since at least 2016.
beats.means: The agency sees the shortage turning into a surplus as other suppliers fill the gap and high prices cut use. Thin stocks mean a new supply hit, like the attacks on Saudi sites this week, can still push prices up fast.
beats.fx: A coming surplus weighs on oil over the months ahead, a mild drag for oil exporters such as Canada and a small relief for importers like Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: The IEA sees supply running ahead of demand from this quarter on.
A softer oil outlook trims support for Canada's main export.

items.watch: Whether Gulf exports keep recovering or new attacks on Saudi sites and tankers cut supply again; OPEC's own monthly report.

items.headline: Eurozone Q3 GDP unchanged in second estimate as uneven growth clouds the outlook
items.story_title: European Central Bank: one more rate rise, then a pause?
items.summary: A second look confirmed the euro area grew 0.4% in the third quarter, but most of that came from Ireland while Germany barely grew and France shrank.

beats.was: The first estimate of euro-area growth for July to September, out in October, showed 0.4%, twice what economists had expected. The European Central Bank kept its deposit rate at 2.5% in October with inflation near 3.8%.
beats.happened: The second estimate left growth at 0.4% from the quarter before and 1.3% from a year earlier. Ireland grew about 5.5%, while Germany managed 0.2%, Italy was flat and France slipped 0.1%.
beats.means: Ireland's figures swing with big multinational companies, so the core of the euro area is weaker than the headline. That does little to stop an ECB rise in December, which is about inflation, but it argues against many more after it.
beats.fx: Gives the euro no new lift; growth in the big economies is soft while the US Federal Reserve looks set to keep raising rates.

impact.why: Growth confirmed at 0.4%, but most of it came from Ireland, not the big economies.

items.watch: Euro-area inflation for November and what ECB officials say about rises after December.

items.headline: Dollar set for best week in two months on rate hike wagers, yen tests 160
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The dollar is heading for its biggest weekly gain since September, as markets start to price a chance that the Federal Reserve raises rates by half a point rather than a quarter. The Australian dollar has been the weakest major currency over the past month.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve has been raising rates to fight inflation, and a hot US consumer price report earlier this week made investors expect more rises. The dollar was already at its highest since April 2025.
beats.happened: Over the week the dollar gained close to 1% against a basket of major currencies. Futures now show a small chance of a half-point Fed rise at the next meeting, where a week ago there was none, and two-year US Treasury yields jumped sharply over two days. The yen sat just under 160 per dollar, and the Australian dollar has lost about 2.5% in a month.
beats.means: Money keeps moving toward the dollar because US rates look set to climb faster and further than elsewhere. Australia stands out as the one major economy where markets expect rate cuts next year, which leaves its currency with the least support.
beats.fx: Supports the dollar against most majors; weighs most on the Australian dollar and keeps the yen near the level where Japan has stepped in before.

impact.why: Bets on bigger and more Fed rate rises are pulling money into the dollar.
The only major currency where markets expect rate cuts next year, so it has the least rate support.
The wide gap between US and Japanese rates keeps the yen near 160 per dollar.
The euro is near its lowest against the dollar since April 2025.

items.watch: Friday's US producer price report and next week's Fed speeches: softer price data would cool talk of a half-point rise.
